newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU farm chief calls for independent food agency.
newsitem.headline: EU farm chief calls for independent food agency.

text.p: European Union Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler on Monday urged member states to show their commitment to protecting consumer health by finding the money to create an independent agency to guarantee food safety,

Fischler, anxious to head off scathing criticism from a European Parliament committee of inquiry about alleged mishandling of the mad cow crisis, challenged the 15 states to support stricter food safety measures.
"It seems that member states when it comes to strengthening and broadening EU checks are not much interested...," Fischler told a news conference ahead of a meeting of EU farm ministers.
"This will need more than mere paying of lip service to political intentions," he added. "If you don't have the money you don't have the controls,"
Fischler complained that a Commission proposal in May to create a European veterinary and plant health agency in Ireland was grounded by lack of funds.
Some member states are reluctant to hand over more power to Brussels in such a sensitive area.
Fischler estimated that the new agency would need about 100 inspectors, compared with 30 in the current unit within the Commission's powerful directorate general for agriculture.
"We have to guarantee the independence of any monitoring," he insisted, adding this meant it must be separated from the EU's executive and have a separate budget.
Fischler said the new veterinary and plant health inspection agency could be modelled on the EU's financial watchdog, the Court of Auditors.
"It works in a very sensible way with the Commission...why can't we have that kind of system applied in other areas ?" he asked.
Fischler said it was a more appropriate model than the United States Food and Drug Administration which did not cover all food sectors. For instance it left meat to the agriculture ministry.
Reiterating testimony to the parliamentary inquiry on December 3, Fischler stressed it was up to member states to ensure that EU food safety measures were enforced.
"The Commission is not a police force monitoring every citizen or company," Fischler said.
Taking on board criticisms from the inquiry, Fischler said that the way in which the EU took scientific advice could be improved.

The appointment of scientific advisers, their political independence, time limits for delivering opinions, need for full-time committee managers, coordination of advice from different committees needed to be examined, he said.

The Parliament, which has just finished interrogating EU commissioners, national officials and scientists, is expected to demand a major shake-up of the Commission's veterinary services to end a conflict of interest.
The services are controlled by the agricultural directorate which handles 50 percent of the total EU budget.
During the past three months the inquiry has pointed an accusing finger at the Commission and Britain, saying they gave priority to producers and profits over public health.
The Parliament's report is due in February 1997.
